sections.title: Balaam's Prophecy of Israel's Greatness
observations: In this section, Balaam, a non-Israelite prophet, is summoned by Balak, the king of Moab, to curse Israel. However, instead of cursing them, Balaam is compelled by God to bless Israel. This highlights God's sovereignty over the nations and His protective hand over His people.
Balaam's prophecies reveal the unique status of Israel as God's chosen people. The imagery used emphasizes their strength and the divine favor they possess, which cannot be undone by human schemes.

sections.title: The Future of Israel and the Nations
observations: Balaam continues to prophesy about the future of Israel, indicating that they will be a powerful nation that will ultimately triumph over their enemies. This serves as a reminder of God's promises to Abraham and his descendants.
The mention of Israel's enemies and their eventual downfall serves to reassure the Israelites of God's faithfulness. It also serves as a warning to those who oppose God's people.

sections.title: The Star and Scepter Prophecy
observations: In this climactic prophecy, Balaam speaks of a star coming out of Jacob and a scepter rising out of Israel. This is often interpreted as a messianic prophecy, pointing to the coming of Christ, who will establish His kingdom.
This section emphasizes the hope and future glory of Israel, as well as the ultimate victory of God's plan through the Messiah.

sections.title: Balaam's Final Words and Departure
observations: After delivering these powerful prophecies, Balaam departs, but not before acknowledging the futility of opposing God's will. His departure signifies the end of his role in this narrative, leaving a lasting impact on both Balak and Israel.
This conclusion serves as a reminder that God's purposes will prevail, regardless of human opposition.

importantVerses.commentary: 'Blessed is everyone who blesses you, and cursed is everyone who curses you.' This verse encapsulates the theme of divine favor and the consequences of opposing God's chosen people.

'I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.' This verse is significant as it points to the coming Messiah and the establishment of His kingdom.

questions: What does Balaam's inability to curse Israel teach us about God's sovereignty?
How do Balaam's prophecies reflect the future hope of Israel and the coming Messiah?
In what ways can we see the fulfillment of these prophecies in the New Testament?
